Straight from the Q1 retro, Devi's exact words:

> *"I do not want to be the company that buys ads for the word 'observability'. I want to be the company you find because the README is the cleanest one you read this month."*

That quote is the brief. She wants Plinthworks discovered through **documentation quality**, not paid keywords.

A few things she's been consistent on across calls and retros:

- **Docs as the product surface.** For her ICP (head of platform at a Series B, paged twice this quarter), the docs are evaluated before sales ever gets a call. Marcus operationalized this with an editorial gate — he signs off on every technical claim before anything ships.
- **Specificity over category.** She killed the "what is an API" framing at the positioning workshop: *"I need a landing page that explains why ours does not page the on-call."* The buyer is not learning what the category is — they have already been paged by it.
- **Organic before paid.** She told Leo directly: *"Let me see organic move first. If the post does not work without spend, the ad will not work either."* Paid is confirmation, not discovery.

The through-line: she wants the technical credibility of the README, the docs voice, and the homepage copy to do the work. Being found = being the clearest, most technically honest voice in the category. Not the loudest buyer of the keyword.

Here's the full picture from what we have on record:

**Who Plinthworks is selling to now**

The buyer is the **head of platform at a Series B company** — someone who has been paged twice this quarter for the exact category Plinthworks operates in. Devi said "observability" six times in the kickoff. Not as a buzzword. She meant the dashboards she is watching at 2am when a customer hits the on-call channel.

Her verbatim positioning anchor, filed as the Plinthworks homepage brief:

> "I do not need another landing page that explains what an API is. I need one that explains why ours does not page the on-call."

**Who Devi said to stop writing for**

**Indie developers.** She corrected us twice on the same call. Direct quote:

> "We are not selling to indie devs anymore. The buyer is the head of platform at a Series B who has been paged twice this quarter for our category."

This is logged as a kill criterion in the belief pattern — not a preference, a hard rule. She will not let the funnel keep speaking to the previous audience.

**The internal tension worth watching**

Priya (growth side) keeps pulling toward reach and launch content engagement. Devi is asking about pipeline. Those two metrics are pointed at different buyers. Maya now routes copy through Devi's senior on-call engineer before staging because Devi's rule is that no marketing post ships until two engineers have signed off on the technical claim.

The short version: write for someone who gets paged at 2am. If the copy would not make that person stop scrolling, it does not ship.

agentRun.finalAnswer:
**Marcus wins. Here's why the evidence is definitive.**

## The Decision is Already Made

Marcus closed the thought-leadership thread with one line: *"If we are writing posts our own engineers would not read, we are wasting Devi's time."* Devi responded with a single check-mark emoji. That was editorial policy by acclamation. It is not a debate — it is a standing rule.

## Why Priya's Direction Loses

The brain has already surfaced this exact failure path:

- **Engagement on the launch post was high. Pipeline was flat.** That is not a win — it is the lesson.
- Priya is chasing reach. Devi's stated metric is **platform-buyer demos**: heads of platform at Series B companies who get paged for on-call incidents.
- Priya has said "we just need more launch content" twice on the same call. The number she wants to be measured on is impressions. The number Devi cares about is qualified pipeline.
- This is a documented pattern: secondary stakeholders with reach metrics drift brand inside 90 days.

## The Actual Editorial Standard for Plinthworks

Every piece of content must clear **two gates** before it ships:

1. **The engineer test** — would their own platform engineers read it and find it credible?
2. **The claim gate** — Marcus signs off on every technical claim; no post ships without engineer assent.

Thought-leadership that does not pass gate one gets killed. Launch content that chases reach over pipeline feed the wrong ICP.

## What to Recommend

Tell Priya the brief stays anchored to the on-call buyer. If she wants more volume, the path is **more technically precise content** — incident response narratives, staging rollback examples, observability benchmarks with real p99 numbers — not broader reach posts.

Reach without pipeline is the disqualified pattern. Plinthworks does not pay for it.

Here's what the brain has on Cloverkin lifecycle rules, synthesized into actionable send-window rules for Sara this week.

---

## Cloverkin Lifecycle Send-Window Rules
**Owner: Sara | Effective: This week**

---

### The Non-Negotiable

> "I would rather lose the visit than send a marketing email a patient finds in their inbox the day after a hard appointment."
> *— Dr. Marisol Vega*

This is not a preference. It is a trust violation rule. Missing the send window is better than breaking it.

---

### Rule 1: 48-Hour Post-Visit Blackout

**No marketing send within 48 hours of any patient appointment.**

- Pull the visit calendar before finalizing any send list.
- Suppress any patient with an appointment in the prior 48 hours.
- This applies to all send types: nurture, re-engagement, check-in.
- The lifecycle tool has this enforced in logic already. Verify it is active before any batch goes out.

---

### Rule 2: No Urgency Modifiers

Remove any language that creates time pressure. Cohort nurture was only approved after urgency modifiers were stripped. The same bar applies here. Words like "last chance," "act now," "don't miss" do not survive the bedside test.

---

### Rule 3: The Bedside Test (Copy Gate)

Before any email goes to send, read it imagining a patient at 11pm after a difficult appointment. Ask: does this lower their heart rate or raise it?

If a clinician would wince reading it aloud, it does not ship.

---

### Rule 4: Clinical Outcome Language = Escalate

Any copy that mentions patient outcomes, results, or clinical claims triggers a double review: Maya (brand voice) plus James (clinical). Do not send until both are logged. This is not a late gate — it is the brief.

---

### Rule 5: Paid Has a Two-Week Organic Window

Cloverkin metro posts are on a two-week organic window before any paid talk. If a lifecycle message is being considered for paid amplification, it needs two weeks of organic proof first. Flag anything this week that is approaching that window.

---

### Rule 6: When Timing Is Unclear, Go to Ops

Rachel (patient ops director) ends timing debates with phone data. If Sara is uncertain whether a send window is clean, she escalates to ops before sending. Never guess on visit cadence.

---

### This Week's Checklist for Sara

- [ ] Pull this week's patient appointment calendar before Wednesday send prep
- [ ] Run suppression check: remove anyone with a visit in the prior 48h
- [ ] Run bedside test on all subject lines and preview text
- [ ] Confirm lifecycle tool 48h gate is active (verify in ops)
- [ ] Flag any copy with clinical outcome language for Maya + James review
- [ ] Check any content approaching the two-week organic window for paid consideration

---

Two things worth flagging for your Wednesday partner sync: confirm whether the 48h suppression list is pulling from real-time appointment data or a manual export, and verify whether Sara has visibility into appointment cancellations (a cancelled appointment is still a hard day). Worth closing that gap this week before a send lands wrong.

agentRun.finalAnswer:
Dr. James Ouedraogo uses the **heart-rate test**.

His exact words from the eligibility-page review:

> *"Patients read this when they are scared. Cut every word that does not lower the heart rate."*

That sentence became the standing test in the lifecycle SOP. Every patient-facing send is now reviewed against it before it ships.

A few things worth noting about how he applies it:

- **Medical accuracy comes before tone.** In the first patient draft he reviewed, three of his four circles were accuracy issues, one was tone.
- **Clinical wince test runs alongside it.** If a clinician would wince reading it aloud, it doesn't ship.
- **He reviews faster than most copywriters.** Clinical lens has trained sharp brand intuition — he catches the tone miss as quickly as the accuracy miss.
- **It's baked into the SOP.** Sara formalized the heart-rate filter as an explicit checkpoint in the send-window process.

Bottom line: before any Cloverkin patient-facing copy goes out, it has to pass one question — does this lower the heart rate of someone reading it on a hard day?
